opus-5.5.text:
I think there are really three requirements, and they pull against each other a bit.

The first is speed. Reinforcement learning is extremely sample-hungry. A policy might need hundreds of millions or even billions of interaction steps before it learns something robust, and you simply cannot collect that on real robots. So the simulator has to run much faster than real time and scale in parallel, thousands of environments on GPUs at once. If it's slow, RL is basically off the table, no matter how beautiful the simulation looks.

The second is fidelity, and here I'd split it into two parts. One is physical fidelity: contact, friction, deformable objects, the dynamics of the actuators themselves. For locomotion we've gotten quite good at this, which is why sim-to-real works so well for legged robots now. For manipulation it's much harder. The moment a hand grasps something soft, or slides an object across a table, the contact models start to break down, and the policy learns to exploit those errors. The other part is perceptual fidelity: if the policy takes camera input, the rendering has to be close enough to reality, in lighting, materials and sensor noise, that what it learns visually actually transfers.

The third, which people often underestimate, is diversity and scalability of content. Having one accurate kitchen isn't enough. You need thousands of scenes, objects, layouts and task variations, plus domain randomization over physical parameters, so the policy generalizes instead of memorizing one environment. Building those assets by hand doesn't scale, so increasingly the question is whether we can generate scenes and objects automatically, sometimes with generative models, and still keep them physically valid.

The tension is that speed and fidelity trade off directly: more accurate contact and rendering cost more compute. So in practice the real requirement isn't perfect simulation. It's simulation that is accurate enough in the dimensions that matter for a given task, fast enough to feed RL, and varied enough that the remaining gap to reality looks to the policy like just one more variation it has already seen. That's the bar I think embodied simulation needs to reach.

r001.rationale: The candidate stresses fast, repeated interaction with environments, but does not identify closed-loop simulation as a requirement.

r002.rationale: It explicitly calls for simulation to “scale in parallel” across “thousands of environments on GPUs at once.”

r003.rationale: It contrasts locomotion with manipulation difficulty, but does not compare embodied-intelligence simulation requirements with autonomous driving.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When people ask what a simulator needs in order to actually support reinforcement learning for robots, I think of it as three things, and they pull against each other.

The first is speed. RL is enormously sample-hungry. A locomotion policy might need hundreds of millions of environment steps before it converges, and if you're running one physics instance at real time, you'll be waiting years. So the simulator has to be massively parallel, ideally thousands of environments running on a GPU in a single process, with the physics, the sensor rendering, and the reward computation all staying on the device so you're not shuttling data back and forth. That's really what changed the field over the last few years. Once you could get tens of thousands of steps per second on one card, things that used to take a cluster became something a grad student could do overnight.

The second is fidelity, and this is where it gets subtle, because fidelity isn't one number. For a quadruped learning to walk, you need contact dynamics to be roughly right, you need the actuator model to resemble a real motor with its torque limits and latency, but you don't actually need photorealistic rendering. For a manipulation task where the policy sees through a camera, it's the reverse. Visual realism and the way lighting, textures, and occlusion behave matter a lot, and you also need deformable objects, cloth, liquids, things rigid-body engines handle badly. So the requirement is really that fidelity be tunable along the dimensions the task cares about, rather than maximized everywhere, because every bit of fidelity you add costs you on the speed axis.

The third is what I'd call closing the gap, and this is about the transfer to the real world. A perfectly fast, reasonably accurate simulator still produces policies that fail on contact when you deploy them, because the real world has friction coefficients, mass distributions, and sensor noise that you didn't model exactly. So the simulator has to support domain randomization natively, meaning you can perturb physical parameters and visual appearance per environment, per episode, cheaply. And increasingly, it needs to support system identification in the other direction, where you take real-world logs and fit the simulator's parameters to them so the distribution you're randomizing over is actually centered on reality.

There are a couple of things beyond those three that I think get underrated. One is asset and scene generation. The bottleneck in a lot of labs now isn't the physics engine, it's building thousands of diverse, physically plausible scenes with articulated objects that have the right joint limits and the right affordances. That's a content problem as much as a simulation problem, and it's where generative models are starting to help. The other is differentiability. If the simulator can give you gradients through the dynamics, you can sometimes replace a lot of brute-force sampling with much more efficient optimization, though that's still fragile around contacts.

And honestly, the last requirement is a boring one: reproducibility and good engineering. Deterministic seeds, stable APIs, the ability to checkpoint and replay a trajectory exactly. RL is already hard to debug, and a simulator that introduces its own nondeterminism makes it nearly impossible to tell whether your algorithm is broken or your environment is.

So if I compress it: fast enough that sample inefficiency isn't fatal, accurate in the dimensions that matter for the task, and designed from the start around the fact that the real world will differ from whatever you built.

r001.rationale: The response discusses simulator speed and RL environment steps, but does not identify closed-loop simulation as a requirement.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the simulator should be massively parallel, ideally running thousands of environments on a GPU.

r003.rationale: The response does not compare these requirements with autonomous driving or say they are much harder.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to treat simulation as a training environment, rather than simply a way to demonstrate a robot’s behavior. For reinforcement learning, that brings several requirements.

First, the physics needs to capture the interactions that matter for the task. If a robot is learning to grasp something, contact, friction, and the object’s response are crucial. A scene can look very realistic and still teach the robot the wrong behavior.

Second, simulation has to be fast and scalable. Reinforcement learning requires a lot of trial and error, so you need to run many environments in parallel, reset them efficiently, and collect experience at high throughput. There’s a tradeoff between physical accuracy and speed, and that tradeoff should depend on what you’re trying to learn.

Third, you need diversity. If training always uses the same object, lighting, and physical parameters, the policy may just learn that particular simulator. You want variation in the environment, sensor noise, delays, and dynamics so that the behavior is more robust.

Finally, you need a way to validate transfer to the real robot. A high reward in simulation isn’t sufficient. You have to test whether the learned behavior works in reality, identify the gaps, and use those results to improve the simulator. So I’d see it as a continuous loop between simulation, training, and real-world testing.

r001.rationale: It describes a continuous loop between simulation, training, and real-world testing, using test results to improve the simulator.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says to run many environments in parallel for reinforcement-learning trial and error.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the difficulty of these simulation requirements with autonomous driving.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that the simulator has to support learning, not just produce a convincing demonstration. For reinforcement learning, you need a lot of interaction, so simulation has to be fast, stable, and able to run many environments in parallel.

Then there’s physical fidelity. The robot’s actions need to produce meaningful consequences, especially for contact, friction, and manipulation. Visual realism alone isn’t enough. You also need usable sensor models and control interfaces, including things like noise and latency, so the policy doesn’t learn to depend on conditions that won’t exist on a real robot.

The third requirement is diversity. You need to vary objects, environments, initial states, and physical parameters, and make it easy to define tasks, rewards, and success conditions. Otherwise, a policy can become very good at one narrow simulated setup without learning a transferable skill.

Ultimately, I would judge the simulator by whether the policies trained in it work in the real world. That means balancing fidelity with throughput, and improving the parts of the simulation that actually affect transfer.

r001.rationale: It says reinforcement learning requires extensive interaction and that actions must produce meaningful consequences, which communicates closed-loop simulation.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the simulator should run many environments in parallel.

r003.rationale: It does not compare the difficulty of embodied-intelligence simulation requirements with autonomous driving.
